name: Fort Napoléon des Saintes
label: Fort Napoléon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort Napoléon' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/42101783: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Napoléon' (197 m across).
notes: Hilltop fortress with a museum, an exotic garden and sweeping views over the bay.

text.description: Fort Napoléon sits on a bluff called the Mire, 119 m above sea level, on Terre-de-Haut in the Îles des Saintes. That height is the reason to come. The fort looks out over the bay and the neighbouring islands, and its high walls and bastions give you strong shapes to frame a view with. A first fort, Fort Louis, was built here between 1777 and 1779. British forces destroyed it in 1809, and the present fortress was built on its ruins. Work started in 1816, and the bastioned design was finished in 1867. It never saw battle and was used as a penitentiary instead. Today it holds a museum about the history, culture and environment of the Saintes, and a botanical garden of local succulent plants and iguanas. For photos, the northern bastion is the best place to start, with a wide view over the bay and the islands around it. The walls and the cactus garden also make a good foreground, with the sea behind. Take a few wide shots for the view, then a few close ones of the plants and stonework. Check which parts of the grounds are open to visitors when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: The fort stands on the Mire bluff on Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes, Guadeloupe. It looks over the bay and the approach to the roadstead.
text.directions_text: Head for the fort on its hill above the bay on Terre-de-Haut. The fort stands on a hill, so expect a climb. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the fort grounds, so once you are inside you are already there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the bay and the sweep of the walls. Use the default lens (1x) for the bastion and the cactus garden. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the islands in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the wide view across the bay and the surrounding islands, walk to the northern bastion, which is the best vantage point within the fort.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, keeping it level. Use a bit of the bastion wall at the edge of the frame to add depth. For a second picture, point down at the fort's walls and cactus garden in the foreground, with the open sea and bay behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far islands to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue. Try panorama mode along the bastion, moving slowly and keeping the phone level. Hold your phone away from the wall edge when you lean out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and clearer colour on the sea. Midday sun can wash out the view.

text.access_note: The fort is a museum and botanical garden, so access may be ticketed or limited; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The fort stands on a hill, so expect a climb to reach it (inferred from the bluff height).
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and gives better colour over the sea than midday sun.

name: Notre Dame de l'Assomption, Les Saintes
label: Church of the Assumpti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place du Gouverneur Lion' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Place du Gouverneur du Lion' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/125182132: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Église Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption' (38 m across).
notes: Village church with a bright red roof in the town centre.

text.description:
Notre-Dame de l'Assomption is the parish church of Terre-de-Haut, an island of Les Saintes. It stands in the village a short walk from the harbour, which makes it an easy first photo after you step off the ferry. Check on the ground that you are in the right spot. From there you can photograph the church front with some of the village around it, so the building has context.

The parish was dedicated to the Virgin of the Assumption to mark the French victory over English troops on 15 August 1666, and Our Lady of the Assumption became the patron saint of Terre-de-Haut. The church has been listed as a national heritage monument (Monument historique) since 31 December 1979. Its bell tower was destroyed in the 2004 earthquake and later rebuilt. The fourth of its four bells was installed on 23 April 2006 at the end of that work.

For your phone, keep the whole front in one frame and watch for people and scooters passing in the foreground. If you want a different angle, the Route de Marigot shows the church front and side from the road. Once you have the wide view, step closer for details of the tower and the entrance.
text.geographic_location: The church is in rue Jean Calot, in the Fond-du-Curé quarter of Terre-de-Haut, in the village close to the harbour. Check on the ground.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or bus stops are listed for this island, and the village is reached on foot. The church is then to the south. Check on the ground that you can see the church before you start shooting. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the church front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or parked vehicles stop you stepping back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for the bell tower and the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place du Gouverneur Lion. A view of the church's front from the ferry-landing square, based on a photo filed under that square's name. Place du Gouverneur Lion is the likely nearby square, but check on the ground. If the spot is busy, the Route de Marigot is a second position, showing the front and one side from the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the church on one of the vertical lines, with the tower upright and not leaning. Keep a little street or square in the bottom of the frame to show how close the church is to the harbour. Take one wide shot, then one zoomed shot of the tower. If you try the Route de Marigot, use the angle to include some of the side of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the tower does not turn white. Check the verticals in the preview before you move on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the front. Midday sun can be flat and bright, so check the result on your screen.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but this is a working place of worship, so ask locally before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Pompierre Beach
label: Pompierre Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plage de Pompierre' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plage de Pompierre' (way/58521854): middle (283 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3390856: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Sheltered white-sand beach on the east side of the island.

text.description: Pompierre Beach is a long curve of pale sand on the north-east side of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes. It runs for about 800 metres along Pompierre Bay. It is the beach most sought after by tourists, and it is planted with coconut trees. A small islet, Les Roches percées, sits offshore and shelters the bay from the trade winds. The rocks also give your photos something to look at beyond the water. The bay is a classified natural site under a French law of 2 May 1930, and motor boats and sailing boats may not enter or anchor in it. That keeps the water free of boats, so your frame stays clean and uncluttered. For a phone, the best picture is simple: palms and carbets (the small shelters) in the foreground, pale sand leading the eye, then the turquoise cove with the pierced rocks behind. Walk a little way along the sand until a palm trunk or a carbet sits on one side of the frame, then shoot out to sea. If you are up for a hike, the Batterie Caroline gives a higher view down over the bay and its beach, with Dominica and Marie-Galante in the distance. The trail is on foot only and you will want sturdy shoes and water. Check locally for any closures or restrictions before you go.
text.geographic_location: Pompierre Beach is on the north-east coast of Terre-de-Haut, along Pompierre Bay, in the Pompierre area. The islet of Les Roches percées lies just offshore.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or ferry stops are listed for this spot. Head towards Pompierre, on the north-east side of Terre-de-Haut. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of sand, palms and bay in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the cove with the rocks behind. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pierced rocks and compress the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the sand, facing out toward the bay and the offshore rocks). The white sand, coconut palms and carbets in the foreground, with the turquoise cove and the pierced rocks behind them. From here you see white sand, coconut palms and carbets in the foreground, with the turquoise cove and the pierced rocks behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line, so the sand and palms get most of the frame. Put a palm trunk or a carbet at one edge to give depth, and let the line of the shore lead towards the rocks. As an alternative, the Batterie Caroline gives an elevated view down over the bay and its beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sea or sand to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the white sand does not wash out. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the sand, though the beach is described as fairly uncrowded in general.

text.access_note: Check locally for any closures or restrictions before you go; boats are not allowed into the bay.

name: Îlet à Cabrit
label: Îlet à Cabrit
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/42101793: large area 'Îlet à Cabrit' (1395 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Small island at the entrance of the harbour with the ruins of Fort Joséphine.

text.description: Îlet à Cabrit, whose full name means Goat Island of Les Saintes, is a small island lying just off the north-west of Terre-de-Haut. It partly closes off the bay of Les Saintes, so it makes a natural backdrop to a harbour view, with the water in the foreground and the island's green hump rising behind it. The island is about 1.2 km from east to west and 750 m from north to south. Its highest point is Morne Joséphine, at around 90 m. Three headlands, Pointe à Cabrit, Pointe Sable and Pointe Bombarde, frame three small coves, which gives the shoreline a pleasing, scalloped outline. The island has a defensive past. France built a fort on the hilltop in 1777, later called Fort Joséphine, and the British kept it after they occupied Les Saintes in 1809. It served as a penitentiary from 1851 and as a quarantine station from 1871. For a phone photo, the islet works best as a layered scene: foreground water, the island in the middle and sky above. Because the island is fairly large, there is no need to zoom in a lot. Include a boat, a mooring or a bit of shoreline to give the picture a sense of scale. Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, as sea views look odd when they tilt.
text.geographic_location: Îlet à Cabrit sits in the bay of Les Saintes, about 1 km north-west of the main island of Terre-de-Haut, which it belongs to. It helps form the passages leading to the harbours of Mouillage and Fond-du-Curé.
text.directions_text: The centre of the island is about 354 m to the north-east of that point. If you want to visit the island itself, check local information before you go. The phone icon on the map is about 350 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in as much of the island as possible, along with plenty of sky and sea. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the hilltop or a single cove.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 350 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the horizon on a gridline and let the island fill the middle of the frame. Leave some water in the foreground, and include a boat or a bit of coast for scale. For a wide sweep of the bay, try panorama mode and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the island to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the hill stays rich and green. Wipe the lens first, as sea air leaves a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and better colour on the hill and water. Midday sun can flatten the view and make the sea glare.

text.access_note: Access to the island itself and its fort remains may be restricted or ticketed, so check local information before you go.

name: Mouillage, Terre-de-Haut
label: Bourg harbour
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/9332119319: the OpenStreetMap point 'Le Mouillage'.
notes: Waterfront of the town on the bay of Les Saintes, one of the most beautiful bays in the world.

text.description:
Mouillage is the oldest village on Terre-de-Haut and sits on a natural harbour in the central part of the island. It is also where the main port of the Îles des Saintes archipelago is found, so boats are coming and going all the time. That activity is what makes it so good to photograph: moored yachts, the landing stage, and rows of brightly coloured creole houses climbing the hillside behind the water.

The main square, Place du Gouverneur Lion, lies right on the port. It is a lively spot with bars, shops and souvenir stalls, and plenty of visitors come off the cruise and yacht landing stage. One building worth looking out for is the 'Bateau des îles', a house built into the hill in the shape of a ship's bow. Adolphe Catan built it in 1942, and it is still a home today, so photograph it from the street and keep a respectful distance. The old gendarmerie building in the village is now the archipelago's tourism office, a useful stop if you want local advice.

For a phone, the best picture is the wide view: water in the foreground, boats in the middle, and the colourful houses and green hill behind. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Then move in for smaller shots, such as a single boat against the painted façades, or people strolling on the square. Wipe the lens before you start, as sea air can leave a haze on it.
text.geographic_location: Mouillage is a quartier in the central part of Terre-de-Haut, built around the island's natural harbour and main port. The village square, Place du Gouverneur Lion, sits right on the waterfront.
text.directions_text: No bus or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the port at Mouillage, in the middle of Terre-de-Haut, and continue on foot within the village. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole harbour and hillside, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out boats or house fronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From here you look across towards the harbour and the village.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the water along the bottom third of the frame and let the coloured houses fill the middle, using gridlines to keep the horizon straight. Include a boat or the landing stage as a foreground point of interest. For a second picture, go in closer on the square or the ship-bow house with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky or sea looks washed out. Try a Live Photo on the harbour to catch boats moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. The port is busiest when cruise ships or ferries are in.

text.access_note: The port and square are part of the village, but check the official site before you go for anything ticketed or restricted, such as boat trips or the tourism office hours.

name: Anse Mire
label: Anse Mire
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).

notes: Quiet bay on the north side of the town, seen from the water.

text.description:
Anse Mire is a bay on the north side of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes archipelago in the Caribbean. It suits a simple photograph: a curve of coast, the water in front of it and plenty of sky above. The bay is the subject here, not a single building or monument, so the picture works best as a wide, uncluttered view.

The phone icon on the map is about 200 m north-west of the subject. That gives you a little distance, so you can take in the whole shape of the shoreline instead of only the water at your feet. Face south-east, keep the horizon level and let the curve of the bay lead the eye across the frame.

Start with a wide shot, then take a second one with a tighter crop on the part of the shoreline that looks most interesting to you. If people are in the scene, wait for a moment when they are small figures rather than filling the frame, as they give a sense of scale. Take a few frames in a row, because small changes in the water and the clouds can change the whole picture.
text.geographic_location: Anse Mire is a bay in the northern part of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes archipelago.
text.directions_text: Anse Mire is in the north of Terre-de-Haut. From there the bay is about 200 metres to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the bay. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the coastline and sky in one frame. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it for a close crop of the far shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line rather than in the middle. Let the curve of the shoreline run diagonally through the frame. Keep your phone level so the sea does not slope.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or shoreline to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo to catch moving water or passing people, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and less harsh on the water. Midday sun can make the sea glare and flatten the scene.

text.access_note: Anse Mire is a bay on the coast of Terre-de-Haut, but access to the shore and the paths around it may vary, so check local conditions before you go.

text.description:
Anse Crawen is a quarter on the south-western side of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes archipelago in the Caribbean. It is the least inhabited part of the island, so it makes a calmer stop than the busier places on the map. Come here for a quiet coastal scene rather than a single big landmark: sea, shoreline and open sky, with very little clutter.

The phone icon on the map is about 200 m south-west of the subject. That distance suits a phone well. You can take in the whole setting from a distance and then walk closer for details if you like.

Start wide with the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines. Keep the horizon on a gridline so the sea looks level. Then try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a more spacious view with the sky included. If you want to pick out a boat, a rock or a stretch of shoreline, use the telephoto or zoom (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) rather than walking much closer. A short Live Photo can catch moving water or swaying plants. Because this is the least inhabited part of the island, please be considerate of anyone living nearby.
text.geographic_location: Anse Crawen is a quarter in the south-western part of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes. It is the least inhabited part of the island.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or bus stops are listed for this spot. The area lies on the south-western side of Terre-de-Haut, so start from the more populated parts of the island and head in that direction. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sea and sky, and use the telephoto or zoom (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for details further along the shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Walk a little closer if you want a tighter frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, depending on whether the sea or the sky is more interesting. Include a foreground feature such as a rock, a plant or the edge of the shore to give the picture depth. Keep your phone level so the horizon does not slope.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and detail. Wipe the lens with a soft cloth first, as sea air often leaves a film on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the water. Midday sun can look harsh, so lower the exposure a little if you shoot then.

notes: Sugarloaf-shaped rock at the entrance to the bay, a popular snorkelling area.

text.description:
Pain de Sucre is the best-known rock on Terre-de-Haut, in Les Saintes, Guadeloupe. It stands in the quartier of the same name, a mostly residential area in the south-western part of the island. The quartier is a natural anchorage, and the rock plunges into the bay. The rock is made of basalt columns lined up side by side and dropping straight into the blue water. That mix of dark, ridged stone and bright sea is what makes it work so well on a phone screen.

Two small beaches of white sand and turquoise water, Petite Anse du Pain de Sucre and Anse Devant, are also part of this area. They give you a pale, colourful foreground if you want the rock and the water in one frame.

The phone icon on the map is about 330 m north-west of the subject. That distance suits a phone well. Start with the default lens (1x) to show the rock in its setting, then zoom to 2x or more to pick out the vertical lines of the columns. Keep your phone level, using the gridlines, so the sea stays straight along the bottom. Take a few frames, because small changes in zoom change the look of the rock quite a lot.
text.geographic_location: Pain de Sucre is in the south-western part of Terre-de-Haut, in the residential quartier of the same name. The quartier is a natural anchorage, and the rock plunges into the bay.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head for the south-western part of Terre-de-Haut. The phone icon on the map is about 330 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the rock and the bay together. Go to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the basalt columns closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move down to one of the beaches and want sand or water filling the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 330 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line, with the rock on one of the vertical lines rather than dead centre. Leave some sea around it to show how it rises straight out of the water. For a second, closer shot, zoom in until the vertical columns fill most of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rock to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and white sand do not wash out and the dark stone keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands, as zoomed shots show up any shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and better texture on the columns. Midday sun can flatten the rock and make the sea glare.

text.access_note: Check access conditions for individual beaches or paths on the day.
